question: What is @ParameterizedTest and what sources can you use?
title: @ParameterizedTest JUnit 5 | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **`@ParameterizedTest`** runs the same test body once per input set, replacing copy-pasted near-identical tests. You feed data with a **source**: `@ValueSource` (single literals), `@CsvSource` (input→expected rows), `@MethodSource` (a `Stream<Arguments>` for complex objects), plus `@EnumSource`, `@NullSource`, and `@CsvFileSource`. It needs the `junit-jupiter-params` module.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can remove duplicate tests and match the source to the data shape
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @Test instead of @ParameterizedTest, or @ValueSource when you need input/expected pairs
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Map each source to its use case and mention naming invocations for readable reports

sections.title: One Test Body, Many Inputs
sections.content: A **parameterized test** turns several near-identical tests into one. Mark the method **`@ParameterizedTest`** (not `@Test`) and attach a **source** of arguments. **`@ValueSource`** supplies a single array of literals. **`@CsvSource`** supplies comma-separated rows — ideal for input/expected pairs, with automatic type conversion. **`@MethodSource`** points at a factory returning `Stream<Arguments>` for complex objects or nulls. There's also `@EnumSource`, `@NullSource`/`@EmptySource`, and `@CsvFileSource`. JUnit runs the body once per row, each as its own reported case.

sections.title: How Sources Feed the Test
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB V["@ValueSource
single literals"] --> E["@ParameterizedTest
method"] C["@CsvSource
input -> expected"] --> E M["@MethodSource
Stream"] --> E E --> R["runs once per row,
each a reported case"] ```

sections.title: The Common Sources
Which Source to Use
sections.content:
| Source | Best for | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `@ValueSource` | One argument, simple literals | a list of ints/strings |
| `@CsvSource` | Input→expected pairs inline | `"2, 3, 5"` |
| `@CsvFileSource` | Many rows from a file | `data.csv` |
| `@MethodSource` | Complex objects, nulls | `Stream<Arguments>` |
| `@EnumSource` | All/选 enum constants | `Status.class` |
| `@NullSource`/`@EmptySource` | null/empty edge cases | strings, collections |

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using `@Test`.** Parameters won't be injected; you need `@ParameterizedTest`.
- **Wrong source.** `@ValueSource` carries only one argument; use `@CsvSource` for pairs.
- **Non-static `@MethodSource`.** Factory must be `static` unless using `@TestInstance(PER_CLASS)`.
- **Missing module.** Needs `junit-jupiter-params` (already in `spring-boot-starter-test`).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@ParameterizedTest`** replaces `@Test` for data-driven tests.
- **`@ValueSource`** — one literal per run.
- **`@CsvSource`** — input→expected rows, auto-converted.
- **`@MethodSource`** — `static Stream<Arguments>` for objects/null.
- **Each row** is a separate reported case; name them with `name=`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A parameterized test lets me run the same test body against many inputs, so instead of writing five nearly identical tests I write one. The key is that I annotate the method with ParameterizedTest instead of Test, and then I attach a source that supplies the data.

I pick the source based on the shape of my data. ValueSource is the simplest — a single array of literals, and the method takes one parameter, so it's great for something like a list of words I want to check are palindromes. CsvSource is for input and expected pairs; each row is comma-separated, like two, three, five for an add test, and JUnit converts the types automatically. MethodSource is for complex objects or nulls — I point it at a static factory method that returns a Stream of Arguments, and each Arguments dot of becomes one run. There are also EnumSource for enum constants, and NullSource and EmptySource for those specific edge cases, plus CsvFileSource if the data lives in a file.

Under the hood JUnit runs the body once per row, and each row shows up as its own case in the report, which I can label with the name attribute so it reads clearly.

The common mistakes are accidentally using the plain Test annotation, in which case the parameters never get injected, and reaching for ValueSource when I actually need pairs, which is CsvSource's job. There's also a small gotcha that the MethodSource factory has to be static. The module is junit-jupiter-params, which Spring Boot's test starter already includes. To stand out, I'd map each source to its use case and mention naming the invocations for readable reports.

question: How do you use @CsvSource for testing multiple input-output pairs?
title: @CsvSource JUnit 5 | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **`@CsvSource`** supplies inline comma-separated rows to a `@ParameterizedTest`, perfect for **input→expected pairs**. Each row maps to the method's parameters with **automatic type conversion** (`"2, 3, 5"` → three ints). Quote values containing commas, use `nullValues`/`emptyValue` for edge cases, and add a `name` for readable reports. It collapses many repetitive tests into one table.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can express input/expected tables compactly and handle null/quoting
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting that CSV values auto-convert types, or not quoting values that contain commas
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use nullValues for null cases and a custom name pattern so each row is labelled

sections.title: Input→Expected Tables, Inline
sections.content: **`@CsvSource`** lets you list rows of comma-separated values directly in the annotation; each row becomes one test invocation and each cell maps positionally to a method parameter. JUnit **auto-converts** strings to the parameter types — `int`, `boolean`, enums, even `BigDecimal`. It's the natural fit for **input→expected** tables. Quote a value that contains a comma (`"'1,000', 1000"`), declare `nullValues = "null"` to inject `null`, and set a `name` pattern so each row is clearly labelled in reports.

sections.title: @CsvSource at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|Shape|~Comma rows|each row = one run|cells map to params|positional
blue|Conversion|~Automatic|String -> int/enum|boolean, BigDecimal|no manual parsing
amber|Edge cases|~null & empty|nullValues = "null"|emptyValue|quote commas
violet|Reports|~name pattern|name = "{0} -> {1}"|readable cases|labelled rows

sections.title: Repetitive: one test per case
Compact: one @CsvSource table
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Unquoted commas.** A value like `1,000` splits into two cells unless quoted (`'1,000'`).
- **Expecting manual parsing.** Types auto-convert; don't `Integer.parseInt` the cells.
- **null via empty cell.** An empty cell is `""` or empty, not `null`; use `nullValues`.
- **No name pattern.** Default labels are opaque; set `name` so failures point to the row.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@CsvSource`** — inline comma rows for input→expected pairs.
- **Auto type conversion** — strings become ints, enums, booleans.
- **Quote commas** inside a value with single quotes.
- **`nullValues`/`emptyValue`** for null and empty edge cases.
- **`name` pattern** labels each row in the report.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
CsvSource lets me list comma-separated rows right in the annotation, and each row becomes one run of the test. Each cell maps positionally to a method parameter, so a row like two, three, five lines up with three parameters. The really convenient part is that JUnit converts the types automatically — strings turn into ints, booleans, enums, even BigDecimal — so I don't parse anything by hand.

That makes it perfect for input and expected tables. For example, testing a password validator, I can write rows like abcd1234 maps to true, abc maps to false, and an empty string maps to false, all in one annotation, and the boolean gets converted for me. If I want to add another case, I just add a row instead of copy-pasting a whole test.

There are a few things to handle carefully. If a value itself contains a comma, like a number with thousands separators, I have to quote it with single quotes so it doesn't split into two cells. For null, an empty cell gives me an empty string, not null, so I set the nullValues attribute to tell JUnit which token means null. And I usually set the name attribute to a pattern so each row shows up with a readable label in the report — that way when a row fails, I know exactly which input broke.

The mistakes I'd avoid are forgetting to quote commas, trying to parse the values manually, and confusing empty with null. To stand out, I'd mention using nullValues for null cases and a custom name pattern for labelled rows.

question: How do you test boundary conditions using parameterized tests?
title: Boundary Condition Testing JUnit 5 | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: Boundary testing checks the edges where bugs cluster: for a valid range `[min, max]`, test **min-1, min, max, max+1** (and often 0, empty, and null). Parameterized tests express this as a compact table so you systematically cover the boundaries instead of one happy-path value — most off-by-one bugs live exactly at these edges.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you systematically test edges (off-by-one) rather than a single representative value
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Testing only one in-range value and missing the just-below/just-above boundaries where bugs hide
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention equivalence partitioning + boundary value analysis and the min-1/min/max/max+1 recipe

sections.title: Bugs Cluster at the Edges
sections.content: Most defects are **off-by-one** errors that live at the boundaries of a valid range, not in the middle. **Boundary value analysis** says: for a range `[min, max]`, test the values **just below min, exactly min, exactly max, and just above max**, plus special cases like 0, empty, and null. Parameterized tests make this systematic — one table covers every edge with one test body. This pairs with **equivalence partitioning**: pick one value from each 'class' of inputs (invalid-low, valid, invalid-high) and hammer the edges between them.

sections.title: Boundary Recipe for [min, max]
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart LR A["min - 1
(invalid)"] --> B["min
(valid edge)"] B --> C["mid
(valid)"] C --> D["max
(valid edge)"] D --> E["max + 1
(invalid)"] ```

sections.title: Boundary Table with @CsvSource
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **One value only.** Testing age 40 proves nothing about the 18/65 edges where off-by-one bugs live.
- **Skipping just-outside.** min-1 and max+1 catch `<` vs `<=` mistakes.
- **Ignoring specials.** 0, empty string, null, and overflow values often break separately.
- **Vague labels.** Without a `name` pattern, a failing boundary row is hard to identify.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Bugs cluster at edges** — boundaries, not the middle.
- **Recipe** — min-1, min, max, max+1 (plus a mid value).
- **Specials** — 0, empty, null, overflow.
- **Parameterized table** covers all edges in one test.
- **Pairs with** equivalence partitioning.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The core idea behind boundary testing is that bugs cluster at the edges of a valid range, not in the middle. Most of them are off-by-one errors — using less-than where you meant less-than-or-equal, that kind of thing. So testing one value in the middle of the range proves almost nothing about where the bugs actually live.

The technique is boundary value analysis. For a valid range from min to max, I test four key points: just below min, exactly min, exactly max, and just above max. I usually throw in a clearly valid middle value too. So if a rule says an age has to be between eighteen and sixty-five inclusive, I'd test seventeen as invalid, eighteen as valid, sixty-five as valid, and sixty-six as invalid. The seventeen and sixty-six cases are what catch the off-by-one mistakes. I'd also add special cases that often break on their own — zero, negative numbers, empty strings, null, and overflow values like Integer max.

Parameterized tests are the perfect tool for this, because I can put all those edges into a single CsvSource table and run one test body against all of them. That makes the coverage systematic and easy to read, and adding a boundary is just another row. I give it a name pattern so each row is labelled, because when a boundary fails I want to know immediately which one.

This pairs with equivalence partitioning, where I group inputs into classes — invalid-low, valid, invalid-high — and pick representatives, then focus on the edges between them. To stand out, I'd name both techniques and give the min-minus-one, min, max, max-plus-one recipe.

question: How do you use @MethodSource for complex parameterized test arguments?
title: @MethodSource JUnit 5 | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **`@MethodSource`** supplies arguments from a factory method returning a **`Stream<Arguments>`** (or `Collection`/`Iterator`). Use it when arguments are **complex objects, computed values, or include nulls** that `@CsvSource` can't express. The method must be **`static`** (unless `@TestInstance(PER_CLASS)`) and named to match the source, building each case with `Arguments.of(...)`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can provide rich object arguments and know the static/naming rules
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Non-static factory method, name mismatch, or using @MethodSource when @CsvSource would be simpler
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use Arguments.of for typed objects and note the factory can be shared/external (FQN reference)

sections.title: Arguments from a Factory Method
sections.content: **`@MethodSource`** points at a **factory method** that returns a `Stream<Arguments>` (or `Collection`, `Iterator`, array). Each `Arguments.of(...)` becomes one invocation, with elements mapped to the test's parameters. Reach for it when the data is too rich for CSV — **domain objects, computed values, nulls, or multiple complex parameters**. The factory must be **`static`** by default (non-static needs `@TestInstance(PER_CLASS)`), and `@MethodSource` with no value defaults to a method matching the test name. You can reference a method in another class by its fully-qualified name.

sections.title: @MethodSource at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|What it is|~Factory method|returns Stream<Arguments>|each = one run|rich data
blue|Build args|~Arguments.of(...)|typed objects|mixed types|nulls OK
amber|Rules|~static by default|name matches if blank|PER_CLASS for non-static|external via FQN
violet|Use when|~CSV too limited|domain objects|computed values|complex combos

sections.title: Complex Objects via @MethodSource
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Non-static factory.** Must be `static` unless the class uses `@TestInstance(PER_CLASS)`.
- **Name mismatch.** Blank `@MethodSource` defaults to a method named like the test; otherwise name it explicitly.
- **Overkill.** For simple literals or pairs, `@ValueSource`/`@CsvSource` are simpler.
- **Wrong return type.** Return `Stream<Arguments>` (or Collection/Iterator), not a raw `Object[]` per element by accident.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@MethodSource`** — factory returning `Stream<Arguments>`.
- **`Arguments.of(...)`** — one row of typed parameters.
- **`static`** by default (non-static needs PER_CLASS).
- **For complex data** — objects, nulls, computed values.
- **External factory** via fully-qualified `Class#method`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
MethodSource is the parameterized source I use when the arguments are too rich for CSV. Instead of inline strings, I point it at a factory method that returns a Stream of Arguments, and each Arguments dot of call becomes one run of the test, with the elements mapped to the test's parameters.

The reason I'd choose it over CsvSource is when my inputs are real domain objects, computed values, or include nulls — things you can't cleanly express as comma-separated text. For example, testing a pricing service, my factory can produce a premium customer with a hundred dollar order expecting ninety, a regular customer expecting a hundred, and an edge case with a zero order. Each of those is an Arguments dot of with actual objects, which is much clearer than trying to encode them as strings.

There are a couple of rules. The factory method has to be static by default — if I want it non-static, I switch the class to the per-class test instance lifecycle. And if I leave the MethodSource value blank, it looks for a method with the same name as the test; otherwise I name it explicitly. A nice feature is that I can also reference a factory in a completely different class using its fully-qualified name with a hash before the method name, which is great for sharing test data across classes.

The mistakes I'd avoid are forgetting the static requirement, getting the method name wrong, and reaching for MethodSource when a simple ValueSource or CsvSource would do. To stand out, I'd mention building typed objects with Arguments dot of and that the factory can live in an external class via the fully-qualified reference.
